chapters.title: Chapter 3: Ajay’s Journey With the Data

episode.tagline: How do we understand the world? Over the last couple of decades, new sources of data have given us great insights into our deep past — and our deep present.
episode.about: In this episode, Amit and Ajay discuss what our genetic data tells us about our prehistory — and how phone battery life can reveal character!

items.content: Ajay introduces 'the great Omit Varma' in Bengali style. Amit replies that to Ajay he's Amit, 'just as you are Ajay and not Ajoy. Two…
Amit, after Ajay's ode to data: 'the road to knowledge begins with data, and I would say the road to knowledge ends in despair.'
On all 7.5 billion humans descending from mitochondrial Eve: 'Why are you laughing? This is a serious subject. But I suspect the lady…
On 3-5% Neanderthal DNA in Europeans and Asians: 'we were having a party with Neanderthals'. So calling someone a Neanderthal who 'won't…
Amit teases Ajay for constantly texting: the crew wonders what he's up to, 'and you always say while you blush, I am checking the…
Amit blames his credit-card fiasco on being Bengali ('because I'm Bengali I'd be lazy'). He has a credit card again only because, 'and…
Before the 4.7% parking-lot statistic, Amit borrows clickbait style: 'you won't believe what happened next.'
On saying 'indexes' rather than the British 'indices': it's sexier, 'because we don't talk of the sises, we talk of the sexes.'
The lipstick index failed during COVID: 'People are wearing masks so they don't need lipstick. You understand what I'm saying? This is a…
Introducing Greenspan's male underwear index, Amit describes him as an economist who 'loved low interest rates'. In bad times the gap…
An unnamed older friend who played chess across Europe and the Soviet Union in the 1980s turned his underwear inside out when it got…
On the hemline index: after the 1973 oil shock maxi skirts came into vogue, 'see the result of bad economics', which Amit finds 'utterly…
On the diaper rash index: 'You simply have to get your babies all the diapers they need, which is a sentence I never thought I'd say.'
The closing 'EIE shirts index' stands at five: Ajay scores 9.5 and black-clad Amit 0.5 ('Black is a state of mind'). When Ajay once…
Kepler and Newton: Ajay's model of science as measurement, then statistical regularities (Kepler's laws), then theory (Newton).
Nineteenth-century bloodletting and the absence of germ theory, which Amit says is why quack treatments like homeopathy flourished: the…
Wittgenstein, invoked by Amit for the idea that language limits how much of the world we can express.
Tagore, whose own translations from Bengali into English don't sound as good, because the two languages hold different values.
G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy and David Hume's is-ought problem, cited against turning human differences into hierarchies.
James C Scott's Seeing Like a State: Ajay quips its alternative title could be 'State Legibility Projects Have Unintended Consequences'.…
'A language is a dialect with an army', the old line Amit uses to explain why Bhojpuri, Maithili and Haryanvi were swallowed by Hindi.
Chandra Bhan Prasad naming his two heroes as Ambedkar and Adam Smith. Amit adds his claim that Manmohan Singh did more for Dalits than…
AlphaZero in chess: humans had to reverse-engineer its play to learn that initiative matters more than they had thought, just as humans…
China's government-run social credit score, which Amit calls 'creepy', contrasted with voluntary phone-data lending.
Sam Walton counting cars in Walmart parking lots to judge his business, the spark for satellite-based alternative data.
Alan Greenspan's view, per Ajay, that better measurement yields far bigger gains than more economic theory.
Hannah Arendt's line that authoritarians run out of people to oppress, invoked by Ajay in the fertility discussion.
Javier Milei, mentioned in the context of Argentina's inflation crisis. Amit says they'll do an episode on him once things settle.
